title: Cough Medicine and Alcohol: Robitussin, Mucinex DM and Safety
excerpt: Can you drink on cough medicine? How dextromethorphan, guaifenesin, antihistamines, acetaminophen and codeine each interact with alcohol, plus Robitussin and Mucinex DM explained.
metaDescription: Can you drink on cough medicine? How DXM, guaifenesin, Robitussin and Mucinex DM interact with alcohol, how long to wait, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** it's best not to drink while you're taking cough medicine. How risky the combination is depends almost entirely on which ingredients are in the bottle. A plain expectorant like guaifenesin (the active ingredient in plain Mucinex) has no well-documented dangerous interaction with alcohol. Dextromethorphan, the "DM" in Robitussin DM and Mucinex DM, adds to alcohol's dizziness, drowsiness, and clumsiness. Night-time formulas with a sedating antihistamine make that much stronger. Multi-symptom products often hide **acetaminophen**, which puts extra strain on your liver when you drink. And prescription cough syrups with **codeine or hydrocodone** should never be mixed with alcohol at all, because the combination can slow or stop your breathing.

**The quick rules:** Read the Drug Facts label before you pour a drink, not after. Never drink with a prescription cough syrup that contains an opioid. Don't drink on a night-time or "PM" cough formula. If your product contains acetaminophen, count it toward your daily limit and don't add Tylenol on top. Take only the labeled dose, and don't use cough medicine to treat a hangover. If someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, confused, or having a seizure after mixing cough medicine and alcohol, call **911**. For questions about a possible overdose, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general pharmacology and the information printed on US over-the-counter labels. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and your full medication list. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before combining cough medicine and alcohol if** you take an antidepressant (especially an SSRI or an MAOI), a sleep aid, an anxiety medicine, a seizure medicine, a prescription painkiller, or any other prescription drug; if you drink 3 or more drinks most days; or if you have liver disease, asthma or COPD, high blood pressure, heart disease, or sleep apnea. **Get emergency help (911) if** someone has slow, shallow, or noisy breathing, can't be woken, has blue or gray lips, is having a seizure, or is severely confused, agitated, or hallucinating.

## Why "Cough Medicine" Isn't One Thing

The phrase "cough medicine and alcohol" covers several very different drugs. A single bottle can contain one active ingredient or five. That's why the honest answer to "can I drink on cough medicine?" is always "which one?"

Here are the ingredients you'll find on most US cough products, and how each one tends to behave with alcohol:

| Ingredient | What it does | Common products | Concern with alcohol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guaifenesin | Expectorant (thins mucus) | Mucinex, Robitussin Chest Congestion | Low. No well-documented dangerous interaction, but alcohol works against it by dehydrating you. |
| Dextromethorphan (DXM) | Cough suppressant | Robitussin DM, Mucinex DM, Delsym, many "DM" store brands | Moderate. Adds to dizziness, drowsiness, and poor coordination. Dangerous at high doses. |
| Sedating antihistamines (doxylamine, diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine) | Dry up drips, cause drowsiness | Night-time and "PM" cough and cold formulas | High. Labels warn that alcohol increases drowsiness. Combined sedation can be heavy. |
| Decongestants (phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine) | Shrink swollen nasal passages | "D" and multi-symptom formulas | Moderate. Can raise heart rate and blood pressure; alcohol can add to a racing, jittery feeling. |
| Acetaminophen | Pain and fever reliever | Multi-symptom cough, cold, and flu products | Moderate to high. Liver strain, especially with heavy drinking or doubled-up doses. |
| Codeine, hydrocodone (prescription) | Opioid cough suppressants | Prescription cough syrups | Very high. Can cause dangerous or fatal breathing problems. Never combine. |

The rest of this guide goes ingredient by ingredient, then covers the two products people search for most: Robitussin and Mucinex DM.

## Dextromethorphan (DXM) and Alcohol: The Main Interaction

Dextromethorphan is the most common cough suppressant in the US. It works in the brain, raising the threshold for the cough reflex. At normal doses it's considered reasonably safe for most adults, and its main side effects are mild: dizziness, drowsiness, nausea, and sometimes a slightly "foggy" feeling.

The trouble is that alcohol causes the same effects. Both act on the central nervous system, and both can slow your reactions and throw off your balance. Put them together and the effects add up. A drink that would normally leave you fine might leave you noticeably lightheaded or unsteady. That matters most if you plan to drive, use stairs in the dark, look after children, or do anything else where a stumble or a slow reaction has consequences.

### Why the effects stack

At normal doses, DXM acts on several brain receptors, including NMDA receptors (part of the brain's main "excitatory" signaling system) and sigma receptors. Alcohol also dampens NMDA signaling, among many other effects. Research in clinical pharmacology describes this kind of overlap as an additive effect: the two drugs don't cause something entirely new, but each one makes the other's side effects stronger.

At high doses, DXM behaves very differently. Well above the label dose, it can cause hallucinations, a detached or "out of body" feeling, a racing heart, high blood pressure, vomiting, and confusion. Adding alcohol to a high dose of DXM raises the risk of passing out, choking on vomit, and dangerous breathing problems. Poison control centers see these cases every year. The simplest rule is never to take more than the label says, and never to use DXM to "feel something" with or without alcohol.

### The antidepressant warning matters more than the alcohol warning

The most serious DXM interaction isn't with alcohol. It's with certain antidepressants. DXM raises serotonin activity in the brain, and so do SSRIs (like fluoxetine, sertraline, and paroxetine), SNRIs, and MAOIs. Combining them can cause **serotonin syndrome**, a potentially dangerous reaction with agitation, sweating, fever, muscle twitching or stiffness, fast heartbeat, and confusion. US DXM labels tell you not to use the product if you're taking an MAOI or have taken one in the past two weeks.

There's a second wrinkle. Your liver breaks down DXM mainly through an enzyme called CYP2D6. Some antidepressants, including fluoxetine and paroxetine, block that enzyme, which can make DXM levels in your blood much higher and longer-lasting than usual. A small share of people are also naturally slow at this step, so a standard dose hits them harder.

If you take an antidepressant and you also drink, you're now stacking three things that affect the brain. That's a conversation to have with a pharmacist before you take a DM product, not after.

## Guaifenesin and Alcohol: Low Risk, But Counterproductive

Guaifenesin is an expectorant. It loosens and thins mucus so your coughs actually clear your chest. It's the only active ingredient in plain Mucinex and in Robitussin's chest congestion products.

There is no well-documented dangerous interaction between guaifenesin and alcohol, and the plain-guaifenesin labels don't carry an alcohol warning. If guaifenesin is the only active ingredient in your product, a drink is unlikely to cause a medical problem.

That doesn't mean drinking is a good idea. Guaifenesin works best when you're well hydrated, which is why the labels tell you to drink plenty of water. Alcohol pushes the other way: it suppresses a hormone called vasopressin that normally helps your kidneys hold on to water, so you urinate more and lose fluid. Thicker mucus and a dry throat are the opposite of what you're trying to achieve. Guaifenesin can also cause mild dizziness, headache, and nausea on its own, and alcohol can make those worse.

The bigger catch is that very few people actually buy plain guaifenesin. Most of the cough aisle combines it with DXM, a decongestant, or acetaminophen, and those are the ingredients that change the answer.

## Robitussin and Alcohol

Robitussin is a brand name covering many different products, which is exactly why searching "can I drink on Robitussin" gives such confusing answers. Before you decide anything, look at the front of the package and then the Drug Facts box on the back.

- **Robitussin Chest Congestion and similar plain-expectorant products** contain guaifenesin only. Low interaction risk, but alcohol works against what the medicine is trying to do.
- **Robitussin DM and the cough-plus-chest-congestion products** combine guaifenesin with dextromethorphan. Expect added dizziness and drowsiness if you drink. Don't drive.
- **Multi-symptom, "severe," and cold-and-flu versions** may add a decongestant like phenylephrine, and some add acetaminophen. If yours contains acetaminophen, the liver warning applies.
- **Night-time versions** may add a sedating antihistamine. These are the ones to be most careful with. The combined sedation with alcohol can be strong, and the labels for sedating antihistamines warn that alcohol increases drowsiness.

Many liquid cough and cold syrups, across brands, have also used alcohol as an inactive ingredient to keep the other ingredients dissolved. Formulations change, and many products are now alcohol-free, so check the inactive ingredients list if this matters to you. It's a small amount per dose, but it's worth knowing, especially if you avoid alcohol completely.

## Mucinex DM and Alcohol

Mucinex DM combines guaifenesin with dextromethorphan in an extended-release tablet designed to last about 12 hours. So the advice is the same as for any DM product: drinking on it is likely to make you dizzier and drowsier than either one alone, and you shouldn't drive.

The extended-release design is the part people miss. A tablet you took with breakfast is still releasing DXM into your system in the evening. "I took it this morning" doesn't mean it's out of your body by dinner. Maximum Strength versions contain a larger dose of both ingredients, so the effects can be more noticeable.

A few other Mucinex products are worth separating out:

- **Plain Mucinex** is guaifenesin only (see the section above).
- **Mucinex D** adds pseudoephedrine, a decongestant that can raise heart rate and blood pressure.
- **Multi-symptom and "Fast-Max" products** often contain acetaminophen and a decongestant, and sometimes DXM too.
- **Night-time products** may add a sedating antihistamine, which is the riskiest combination with alcohol.

If you're not sure which one you have, the active ingredients are always listed at the top of the Drug Facts box.

## Night-Time Cough Medicine and Alcohol: The Combination to Avoid

Night-time and "PM" cough and cold formulas usually get their sleepiness from a sedating antihistamine such as doxylamine or diphenhydramine. These are the same drugs used in many over-the-counter sleep aids. Their labels carry a clear warning that alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness, and tell you to avoid alcoholic drinks while using the product.

This is where the combination moves from "uncomfortable" to "genuinely risky." Alcohol and sedating antihistamines both slow down the brain. Together they can cause heavy sedation, confusion, and poor coordination, and the effect is stronger in older adults. Many night-time formulas also contain DXM and acetaminophen, so you can end up stacking three or four separate interactions in one dose.

Antihistamines also tend to make next-morning grogginess worse. If you drink and then take a night-time cough syrup "to sleep it off," you're likely to wake up feeling more hungover, not less. For more on how one of the best-known night-and-day cold products works with alcohol, see our guide to [DayQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/dayquil-and-alcohol), which goes ingredient by ingredient.

## The Hidden Acetaminophen Problem

Many "multi-symptom" cough and cold products contain acetaminophen, the drug in Tylenol, to handle the sore throat, aches, and fever that come with a cough. Acetaminophen is broken down by the liver, and a small part of each dose turns into a toxic by-product that the liver has to neutralize. Regular heavy drinking makes that harder.

The US label for acetaminophen-containing products warns that severe liver damage may occur if you take more than the maximum daily amount, take it with other drugs containing acetaminophen, or have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using the product.

The real-world risk is doubling up. Someone takes a multi-symptom cough syrup, then Tylenol for a headache, then a night-time cold formula, and doesn't realize all three contain acetaminophen. On a label it may also appear as **APAP**. If your cough medicine contains acetaminophen, count it toward your daily total and don't add another acetaminophen product on top. Our full guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver chemistry, the daily limits, and the warning signs.

## Decongestants and Alcohol

Phenylephrine and pseudoephedrine shrink swollen blood vessels in your nose. They do that by acting on the same kind of receptors that raise heart rate and tighten blood vessels elsewhere in the body, so they can nudge up blood pressure and make some people feel jittery or have trouble sleeping.

Alcohol has its own effects on the heart. It often raises heart rate, and heavy drinking can raise blood pressure. In a healthy adult, one drink on a decongestant isn't usually a crisis, but the combination can leave you feeling wired, flushed, or with a pounding heartbeat. If you have high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid disease, or an enlarged prostate, the decongestant itself already needs a pharmacist's okay, and adding alcohol makes that conversation more important.

## Prescription Cough Syrups: Never Mix With Alcohol

Some prescription cough syrups contain an opioid, usually codeine or hydrocodone, often combined with an antihistamine such as promethazine or chlorpheniramine. These are prescribed for hard-to-control coughs in adults.

**Do not drink alcohol while taking any opioid cough medicine.** Opioids and alcohol both slow breathing, and together they can slow it to a dangerous or fatal level. The FDA requires a boxed warning, its strongest kind, on opioid medicines about the risk of combining them with other drugs that depress the central nervous system, and alcohol is one of those. Opioid cough products are not approved for children.

If you've been prescribed one of these and you've already had a drink, don't take your next dose until you've talked to your pharmacist or doctor. If someone has combined them and is very sleepy, hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has blue or gray lips, call 911.

Another common prescription option, **benzonatate** (often sold as Tessalon Perles), works differently, by numbing stretch receptors in the lungs. It isn't an opioid, but it can cause drowsiness and dizziness, and it's very dangerous if swallowed by young children. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist before combining it with alcohol.

## How Long Should You Wait Between Cough Medicine and a Drink?

There's no single waiting time that applies to every cough medicine, and anyone who gives you one exact number is guessing. A sensible, practical approach:

- **Start with the dosing interval on the label.** If a product is dosed every 4 to 6 hours, its effects generally last about that long in most people. An extended-release tablet labeled "every 12 hours," like Mucinex DM, is designed to stay active for about 12 hours.
- **Allow extra time for DXM if you're a slow metabolizer or take certain antidepressants.** In most people, DXM is cleared within several hours, but in people who are naturally slow at breaking it down, or who take fluoxetine or paroxetine, it can linger far longer.
- **Going the other way, let the alcohol clear before you take a dose.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies widely between people. After a heavy night, that can stretch well into the next day.
- **For prescription opioid cough syrups, ask your pharmacist.** Don't guess with these.

If you notice you're unusually dizzy, sleepy, or off-balance, that's your answer for tonight, regardless of how many hours it's been.

## Should You Drink at All With a Cough or Cold?

Even setting the medicine aside, a cough or cold is a poor time to drink. Here's why:

- **Alcohol disrupts sleep.** It can help you fall asleep faster, but it fragments sleep later in the night and suppresses REM sleep. Rest is one of the few things that reliably helps you recover from a cold.
- **It dehydrates you.** That thickens mucus, dries your throat, and can make a cough feel worse.
- **Heavy drinking weakens immune defenses.** Research on alcohol and immunity has found that heavy drinking impairs several parts of the immune response. A single drink isn't the same as a binge, but it isn't helping either.
- **It can irritate an already sore throat** and worsen acid reflux, which itself can trigger coughing at night.

### What about a hot toddy?

The hot toddy (whiskey, hot water, honey, lemon) is a classic cold remedy. The parts that help are the warm liquid, the steam, and the honey. Honey has some research support for soothing coughs, and warm drinks can ease a sore throat. The whiskey adds nothing medical, and it brings the medicine interactions described above. If you like the ritual, make it without the alcohol, especially if you've taken cough medicine. Don't give honey to babies under one year old.

## Cough Medicine for a Hangover? Not a Good Idea

Some people reach for cough syrup the morning after because it's what's in the cabinet, or because they hope a night-time formula will help them sleep through the worst of it. That's a poor trade.

- **Cough medicine doesn't treat hangover symptoms.** There's no good evidence that DXM, guaifenesin, or antihistamines help with headache, nausea, fatigue, or the general unwell feeling of a hangover.
- **Alcohol may still be in your system.** After a late night of heavy drinking, you may still have measurable alcohol in your blood in the morning, so the interactions above still apply.
- **Hidden acetaminophen and hangover mornings don't mix.** If a multi-symptom product contains acetaminophen, you're adding liver work at a time when your liver is still catching up.
- **Sedating ingredients make the grogginess worse.** A night-time formula can leave you foggier and more uncoordinated than the hangover alone.

If you wake up hungover with a genuine cough or cold, keep it simple: water, food, rest, and the single-ingredient medicine that matches your actual symptom, at the labeled dose. A pharmacist can point you to the right one in a couple of minutes. If your main problem is a headache, our guides to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and Tylenol (linked above) explain the trade-offs between painkillers after drinking.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining cough medicine and alcohol if you:

- Take **antidepressants**, especially SSRIs, SNRIs, or MAOIs (serotonin syndrome risk with DXM)
- Take **sleep aids, anxiety medicines, muscle relaxants, seizure medicines, or opioid painkillers**, all of which add to sedation
- Are an **older adult**, since sedating antihistamines hit harder with age and raise the risk of falls
- Have **asthma, COPD, or sleep apnea**, where anything that slows breathing deserves extra caution
- Have **liver disease** or drink 3 or more drinks most days, if your product contains acetaminophen
- Have **high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid disease, or an enlarged prostate**, if your product contains a decongestant
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding**, where the choice of cough medicine itself should go through your doctor

If any of these apply, a five-minute chat with a pharmacist is worth more than anything you'll read online. They can check your exact product against everything else you take. For a broader look at how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most people who have one drink on a standard dose of a DM cough medicine will just feel a bit more lightheaded and sleepy than usual. But some reactions need medical care right away.

**Call 911 if someone who has mixed cough medicine and alcohol:**

- Is very hard to wake, or can't be woken
- Has slow, shallow, irregular, or noisy breathing (snoring or gurgling that sounds wrong)
- Has blue or gray lips or fingertips
- Has a seizure
- Is vomiting while very drowsy (a choking risk; roll them onto their side)

**Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) or seek urgent care if:**

- Someone took more than the labeled dose of a cough medicine, especially with alcohol
- You notice severe confusion, agitation, hallucinations, a racing or pounding heart, high temperature, heavy sweating, or muscle twitching or stiffness (possible serotonin syndrome, especially in someone who takes an antidepressant)
- You took several products that may all contain acetaminophen and aren't sure of the total, or you notice nausea, vomiting, pain under the right ribs, or yellowing skin or eyes afterward

Poison Control is free, confidential, and staffed by experts around the clock. You don't need to be sure it's an emergency to call.

## A Simple Checklist Before You Drink on Cough Medicine

1. **Find the Drug Facts box** and read the active ingredients.
2. **Opioid (codeine, hydrocodone)?** Don't drink. Full stop.
3. **Sedating antihistamine (doxylamine, diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine) or labeled "night-time" or "PM"?** Skip the drink tonight.
4. **Dextromethorphan ("DM")?** Expect extra dizziness and drowsiness. Don't drive, and if you take an antidepressant, ask a pharmacist first.
5. **Acetaminophen?** Count it toward your daily limit, don't add Tylenol, and don't combine with heavy drinking.
6. **Decongestant?** Be cautious if you have heart or blood pressure problems.
7. **Guaifenesin only?** Low interaction risk, but you'll recover faster with water than wine.

## Looking After Yourself When You Do Drink

Once you're over the cough and back to normal, the usual rules for drinking well apply: pace yourself, eat beforehand, alternate drinks with water, and stop earlier than you think you need to. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also use supplements on nights out. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. It has no role in treating a cough, it doesn't reduce the interactions described in this article, and it's not something to add while you're on cough medicine without checking with a pharmacist. If you want to try DHM on an ordinary night out when you're healthy and not taking cold medicine, a budget-friendly option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it.

## The Bottom Line

- "Cough medicine" covers very different drugs. The risk with alcohol depends on the active ingredients, so read the label first.
- **Guaifenesin alone** (plain Mucinex, Robitussin Chest Congestion) has no well-documented dangerous interaction, but alcohol works against it.
- **Dextromethorphan** (Robitussin DM, Mucinex DM, Delsym) adds to alcohol's dizziness and drowsiness. Don't drive, and talk to a pharmacist if you take an antidepressant.
- **Night-time formulas** with sedating antihistamines are the over-the-counter combination to avoid.
- **Acetaminophen** in multi-symptom products adds liver risk, especially if you drink heavily or double up.
- **Prescription opioid cough syrups and alcohol should never be combined.**
- If someone is hard to wake or breathing slowly, call 911. For dose questions, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking cough medicine?**

It depends on the active ingredients, so it's best to avoid drinking while you're taking any cough medicine. Plain guaifenesin has no well-documented dangerous interaction with alcohol. Dextromethorphan (DM) adds to alcohol's dizziness and drowsiness. Night-time formulas with sedating antihistamines and products with acetaminophen carry bigger risks. Prescription cough syrups with codeine or hydrocodone should never be combined with alcohol.

**Can you drink on Robitussin?**

Robitussin is a brand covering many products. Chest congestion versions with guaifenesin only are low risk, though alcohol dehydrates you and works against the medicine. Robitussin DM adds dextromethorphan, which makes you dizzier and drowsier when you drink. Multi-symptom and night-time versions may add a decongestant, a sedating antihistamine, or acetaminophen, which raise the risk further. Check the Drug Facts box and skip the drink if you're unsure.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol with Mucinex DM?**

It's best not to. Mucinex DM combines guaifenesin with dextromethorphan in an extended-release tablet that lasts about 12 hours, so the DXM is still active long after you take it. Alcohol and DXM together increase dizziness, drowsiness, and poor coordination, so don't drive. If you take an antidepressant, ask a pharmacist before using any DM product, with or without alcohol.

**How long after taking cough medicine can I drink?**

There's no single waiting time for every product. A practical guide is the dosing interval on the label: about 4 to 6 hours for many short-acting products and about 12 hours for extended-release tablets like Mucinex DM. Allow longer if you take antidepressants such as fluoxetine or paroxetine, which can slow how fast your body clears dextromethorphan. For prescription opioid cough syrups, ask your pharmacist.

**What happens if you mix dextromethorphan and alcohol?**

At normal doses, the main effect is extra dizziness, drowsiness, slower reactions, and unsteadiness, because both act on the brain. At high doses of DXM, adding alcohol can lead to confusion, vomiting, passing out, and dangerous breathing problems. Call 911 if someone is hard to wake or breathing slowly, and Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) if someone took more than the labeled dose.

**Is it dangerous to drink with codeine cough syrup?**

Yes. Codeine and hydrocodone are opioids, and opioids combined with alcohol can slow breathing to a dangerous or fatal level. The FDA requires its strongest boxed warning on opioid medicines about combining them with other central nervous system depressants such as alcohol. Don't drink at all while taking an opioid cough syrup, and call 911 if someone who combined them is very sleepy or breathing slowly.

**Can I take cough medicine for a hangover?**

It's not a good idea. There's no good evidence that cough medicine helps hangover symptoms, alcohol may still be in your system the next morning, and many multi-symptom products hide acetaminophen, which adds liver strain. Night-time formulas can make you groggier. Stick to water, food, rest, and a single-ingredient medicine that matches an actual symptom, at the labeled dose.

**Does cough syrup contain alcohol?**

Some liquid cough and cold syrups have used alcohol as an inactive ingredient to keep other ingredients dissolved, though many are now alcohol-free and formulations change. The amount per dose is small. If you avoid alcohol completely, check the inactive ingredients list on the package or ask a pharmacist for an alcohol-free option.
